current_episode.title: Mastering maths assessment - getting the right support to the right students

guest.titre: Assessment Specialist for Numeracy and Mathematics
guest.titre_secondaire: Math Specialist Teacher and Subject Leader
guest.bio_context: Andy Small spent nearly 16 years as a mathematics specialist teaching in both primary and independent prep schools, where he served as a maths leader for the vast majority of his career. He worked with driven and passionate colleagues while managing significant challenges including budgeting limitations and disparities in staff confidence. He joined Renaissance to work on assessment development, bringing firsthand classroom experience to product design focused on supporting individual children and teachers.

context.transcript_excerpt: Hello and welcome to a new series of Education Join the Dots, our podcast covering all things assessment and practice. We hope that you all enjoyed the summer break and have come back feeling refreshed and ready for a new academic year. We are of course GL Assessment or GL education, depending on where you are in the world, a renaissance company providing formative standardised assessments in the UK and Ireland, and over 100 countries worldwide. Now, you may have noticed a slight change to the name of our podcast. However, as always, we'll be discussing all things assessment and practice, as well as addressing some of those prevalent topics from the world of education. So we really hope you enjoy tuning into our second series. I'll go ahead and introduce myself. I'm Sophie Riley, Marketing Manager at Renaissance and lately I've had the amazing pleasure of collaborating with Andy Small, our Assessment Specialist for Numeracy and Mathematics. Together we've been working extremely hard to bring our brand new assessment, the new group Math Test, to life. With over a decade of experience in education, it's something I'm deeply passionate about. I truly believe in the power of reading and learning and stand by the saying, education and knowledge is the one thing that can never be taken away from you. Now, if you listened to our July episode, you'll remember we introduced our new segment, Heard It in the Staff Room. This is where we share your voice notes of the hot topics of conversation which have set tongues wagging, either during those PPA meetings, at the end of the day over a pile of unmarked books, or just in those busy break and lunch times. Here are just a couple of the voice notes we received from our listeners over the summer. Hi, I'm Michael Brown. I've been a primary school teacher for the last seven years. I'm currently working in a school in North Manchester and it is difficult to get math specialists to become teachers. I think because mainly there's so many industries and so many jobs in which, you know, having a background in maths can be really lucrative, especially in the private sector. I think it's really difficult to attract those kinds of people to teaching. And so historically, yeah, we've seen very few people with a maths background, especially in primary school teaching. However, I think more recently, I've seen a few more people who have had a career in some sort of, you know, maths-based background, whether it's like finance or business, and then later in life come to teaching. I know of at least a couple of people who have done that so while i think that has been the case in the past i think that that might be a little bit of a shift um primarily because i think it's seen as that those careers can while they're financially very um good i think perhaps people tend to think that maybe they're not doing something really worthwhile and and teaching perhaps fills that kind of gap Hi, my name is Damien Warren and I am a maths teacher at a secondary school in Leeds called Cardinal Heenan. So one of my challenges that I face in maths is when pupils come to the subject with a negative mindset or having experienced sort of negative influences from past years or that parents sort of have already labelled them as they can't achieve in maths because obviously it's hereditary and that because parents aren't good at maths then neither will their kids and that's probably the biggest challenge a lot of pupils that I sort of teach you know do have their struggles in maths and most of them are down to that lack of confidence but the biggest rewarding aspects of my job is is taking that lack of confidence or that negative mindset and turning it around and when you can show kids that they can succeed and that with work dedication and a positive mindset things will start to click and then you see those light bulb moments happening in class is incredibly rewarding I'm sure that's why so many teachers got into the profession in

pending_qa.q: How does persistent student absence impact GCSE mathematics attainment rates?
pending_qa.r: According to statistics Andy Small cited, approximately 84% of students who were rarely absent in years 10 and 11 secured a GCSE pass at grade four or above in mathematics. However, when children's absence reached 10% of sessions—meaning less than 90% attendance across both years—that figure dropped below 50%, demonstrating a significant correlation between attendance and mathematics achievement.

pending_qa.q: What design principles guided the development of the New Group Math Test?
pending_qa.r: Two key drivers shaped NGMT design: first, ensuring a personalized and stress-free test experience for every individual learner; second, putting the most useful information into teachers' hands so that whether they were experienced, new, confident or lacking confidence, they could make informed decisions to facilitate mathematics learning and progress. The assessment uses an adaptive algorithm that adjusts question difficulty in response to learners' answers as they progress through the test.

pending_qa.q: How can adaptive mathematics assessment reduce anxiety and improve accuracy for student testing?
pending_qa.r: Adaptive assessments remove the one-size-fits-all approach where everybody sits the same questions in the same order. NGMT's adaptive algorithm presents test content perceived to be consistent with each child's capability level, which removes significant stress and anxiety from formal assessment situations. Children are assessed in a more targeted and supported way, which makes the assessment tool more accurate while also improving the overall test experience.

pending_qa.q: What does research suggest are the key areas for developing effective mathematics practice in secondary schools?
pending_qa.r: The Education Endowment Foundation study released in June identified four priority areas: first, teacher skills and expertise; second, targeted interventions and supports using assessment data and personalized practice materials like Renaissance's Freckle; third, impactful practice where data shows outcomes reflect positively what is happening in the classroom; and fourth, program engagement where adaptive testing removes barriers and improves student participation.

pending_qa.q: What proportion of the UK population is estimated to experience developmental dyscalculia?
pending_qa.r: According to the British Dyslexia Association, an average of one or two pupils in every UK classroom experiences developmental dyscalculia, which equates to approximately 6% of all people in the UK being considered number dyslexic. NGMT was designed to support teachers in identifying individuals who might be at risk and highlight the need for further exploration.

pending_qa.q: When was the New Group Math Test first proposed as a concept?
pending_qa.r: The New Group Math Test was first proposed back in 2017 as a seed of an idea. Andy Small recalls being asked questions about the potential for a new math test when he was a user of GL's assessments in schools. The project evolved from that initial concept through multiple stages of development, item writing, review, trialing, and standardization before its release.

pending_qa.q: What is the typical duration of the New Group Math Test assessment?
pending_qa.r: The New Group Math Test takes approximately 45 to 60 minutes for learners to complete. Once students have finished the assessment within this timeframe, schools gain access to a wealth of data including overall maths scores, domain-specific results, and insights across multiple curriculum areas.
